what_this_is: The standing watch on a LIVING issue. These are the findings that would change or kill the piece, carried forward past publication instead of being tested once and forgotten. A kill condition that fires after publication is the process working.
the_promise: The page displays the date of the LAST CHECK, not the last change. 'Last reviewed <date>; nothing has changed' is the honest line and the only one that cannot be told by a page nobody has opened.

questions.question: Has the randomised crossover trial been run?
questions.would_change: Everything. Budzyn is retrospective and observational and its own authors call for exactly this: 'robust prospective studies such as randomized crossover trials'. Allan Tucker said the same in the Science Media Centre roundup. A trial that confirms the six-point fall turns the piece's central caution into a finding; one that does not turns the piece into a story about how a confounded result travelled.

questions.answered_in_part: 2026-08-30, by the outside reviewer, not by us. The randomised crossover trial has NOT been run and W1 stays open. But a prospective, multicentre, registry-based trial with a before/during/after-removal sequence has — Pedersen et al., Endoscopy, online 3 June 2026 — and it found no deskilling. It is now on the page. W1 remains open for the randomised design specifically.

questions.question: Has anything we rely on been corrected or retracted?
questions.would_change: Possibly a paragraph, possibly the piece. This is not paranoid: the most-cited meta-analysis in this literature was retracted in April 2026 after nine months of public criticism, and the ESMO scoping review that synthesises the deskilling evidence mis-cites a mammography experiment to a paper that found the opposite. Every source in sources.json is checked against Retraction Watch and its own journal's notices.

questions.question: Does the scoping review's pathology entry cite the paper its figures actually come from?
questions.would_change: Whether the page can say the review misdescribes three of its included studies rather than two. The review reports 28 pathologists and a 7% overturn rate under time pressure. Those are the figures in Rosbach et al. (arXiv 2411.00998), read at source on 2026-08-30. Source ledger S029 records the review's citation for that entry as Bellahsen-Harrar et al. (2025) in Mod Pathol; the Bellahsen-Harrar paper is PLOS ONE 2025;20(8):e0323270, has EIGHT pathologists, no time-pressure condition and no 7% figure. Either the review attaches Rosbach's numbers to a Bellahsen-Harrar citation, or the transcription into S029 crossed two rows of the review's table. THE PAGE PRINTS NOTHING ABOUT THIS. It is an accusation against named authors and it is not going on a page until somebody opens the review's PDF and reads the pathology row and its reference number.

questions.answer: Both. The review's body cites reference 17 — arXiv 2411.00998, the right paper, under wrong author names and a wrong title. Its Table 1 attributes the same figures to reference 35, Bellahsen-Harrar et al., PLOS ONE 2025;20(8):e0323270, which has eight pathologists, no time-pressure condition and no 7% figure. Our 2026-08-29 note was a correct transcription of the table and silent about the body. Settled by reading the review's PDF end to end; every sentence recorded verbatim in sources.json S029 under VERBATIM.

_seeding_note: The kill conditions seeded four questions and they were the wrong four — they are PRE-PUBLICATION tests, and three of them are already answered. A living issue's watch has to be forward-looking: not 'did we get this right' but 'what would arrive that changes it'. Rewritten by hand, which is the honest use of `init`: it finds the questions, a person turns them into a watch.
